cefr.bandName: Pre-A1, before any English at all

unit.unitOverview:
New sounds: ar, or, ir, er, ow, oi.
These are not short and not long. They are their own sounds.
Two letters. One sound.
Do not sound them out one by one.
unit.learningPath:
Listen to the lesson.
Words: the new sounds and the new words.
Patterns: the sounds, reading, writing.
Read three short texts.
Read out loud. Record it.
Write the words from their sounds.
Practice and quiz. Check your answers.
functions: Say the sound for each new spelling
Read a word that has one in it
Write a word that has one in it
Know where in a word each one goes
Read the new words out loud
Choose between two spellings of one sound

visual.lectureScript:
This is Unit 14. The last of Book A.
These sounds are not short and not long.
They are their own sounds.
Four of them use the letter r.
Listen. Ar. Car. c. ar. Two sounds.
Not c, a, r. Two sounds only.
Next. Or. Fork. f. or. k. Three sounds.
Next. Ir. Bird. b. ir. d. Three sounds.
Next. Er. Her. h. er. Two sounds.
Now listen to those last two again.
Bird. Her. Ir and er.
They are the SAME sound.
Two spellings. One sound. That happens a lot.
You learn which word takes which by reading.
Now two more.
Ow. Cow. c. ow. Two sounds.
It is the sound you make when it hurts.
Oi. Coin. c. oi. n. Three sounds.
One sound, not two. Not o then i.
Two more you will meet in the words.
Ear. Hear. h. ear. Two sounds.
Air. Hair. h. air. Two sounds.
Hear and hair. Listen. Hear. Hair.
They look close. They are not the same.
Hear is what your ears do.
Hair is what grows on your head.
That is all of Book A.
You can read most short words in English.
Book B is next. It has no new sounds.
It has new ways to write the ones you know.
That is Unit 14. Well done.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: The new sounds: ar, or, ir, er, ow, oi
grammar.explanation:
These vowels are neither short nor long.
Each pair is one sound of its own.
Four of them use the letter r.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
ar   as in car     c - ar
or   as in fork    f - or - k
ir   as in bird    b - ir - d
er   as in her     h - er
ow   as in cow     c - ow
oi   as in coin    c - oi - n
grammar.workedExample:
You see ar in a word.
1. Do not read two letters.
2. Read one sound.
3. Say that sound out loud.
4. Now find it in car.
5. Say the sound again there.
grammar.commonMistake:
Sounding out both letters gives no word at all.
car is not c - a - r.
It is c - ar.
grammar.memoryTip: Two letters. Look once. Say once.
grammar.practice:
Say the sound for each one.
1. ar
2. or
3. ir
4. er
5. ow
6. oi
grammar.answerKey:
Check yourself out loud.
Did you say ONE sound each time?
Two sounds means you read the letters, not the spelling.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: Reading a word that has ar, or, ir, er, ow, oi in it
grammar.explanation:
Find the two letters first.
Read them as one sound.
Then read the rest of the word.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
car      c - ar
fork     f - or - k
bird     b - ir - d
her      h - er
cow      c - ow
coin     c - oi - n
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word fork.
1. Look for the two letters.
2. Cover them with your finger.
3. Read what is left.
4. Now put the one sound back in.
5. Join it all. fork.
grammar.commonMistake:
Reading left to right, letter by letter, breaks here.
Look for the pair BEFORE you start.
grammar.practice:
Join the sounds and write the word.
1. c - ar
2. f - or - k
3. b - ir - d
4. h - er
5. c - ow
6. c - oi - n
grammar.answerKey:
1. car
2. fork
3. bird
4. her
5. cow
6. coin
Five or six right? You can read these.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: Writing a word that has ar, or, ir, er, ow, oi in it
grammar.explanation:
Say the word. Break it into sounds.
One of those sounds needs TWO letters.
Count sounds, then write.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
car      c - ar             2 sounds, 3 letters
fork     f - or - k         3 sounds, 4 letters
grammar.workedExample:
You want to write bird.
1. Say it out loud.
2. Break it: b - ir - d.
3. Which sound needs two letters?
4. Write that pair together.
5. Read it back to check.
grammar.commonMistake:
One letter for each sound is wrong now.
The new sound takes two letters.
grammar.memoryTip: Count sounds. Some need two letters.
grammar.practice:
Write the word you hear.
1. bird
2. her
3. cow
4. coin
5. hear
6. hair
grammar.answerKey:
1. bird
2. her
3. cow
4. coin
5. hear
6. hair
Five or six right? Good.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: ir and er say one sound
grammar.explanation:
Two spellings. One sound.
You cannot hear which one a word uses.
You learn that by reading the word.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
ir    bird, girl, first, shirt
er    her, water, under, sister

Say bird. Say her. The same middle sound.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to write the sound er.
1. Say the word out loud.
2. The sound does not tell you the spelling.
3. Think of the word written down.
4. If you have seen it, write what you saw.
5. If not, write er and check later.
grammar.commonMistake:
There is no rule here to learn.
Waiting for one keeps you stuck.
grammar.memoryTip: Same sound. Two spellings. Read to learn which.
grammar.practice:
Say each word. Is the spelling ir or er?
1. bird
2. her
3. girl
4. under
5. first
6. water
grammar.answerKey:
1. ir
2. er
3. ir
4. er
5. ir
6. er
You could not hear it. You had to look. That is the point.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: ear and air: hear and hair
grammar.explanation:
Two more pairs, both with a vowel and r.
They look close and sound close.
The meanings are not close at all.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
ear   hear, near, year, clear
air   hair, fair, chair, pair

hear  what your ears do
hair  what grows on your head
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word hear.
1. Find the pair. It is ear.
2. That is one sound.
3. Say h, then ear.
4. Two sounds. Hear.
5. Now do the same with hair.
grammar.commonMistake:
Hear and hair get swapped constantly.
Read the whole word, not the first two letters.
grammar.memoryTip: Ear is for ears. Air is for hair.
grammar.practice:
Which word fits? hear or hair
1. I can ___ the cow.
2. Her ___ is dark.
3. Did you ___ that?
4. Cut my ___.
5. I cannot ___ you.
6. Wash your ___.
grammar.answerKey:
1. hear
2. hair
3. hear
4. hair
5. hear
6. hair
All six right? You have them apart.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example, every practice has a key, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back, check.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.note: This is the whole unit, and it goes against everything Units 2 to 7 taught. Expect a learner to read the letters separately for a while. Do not explain it again; point at the pair and say the one sound, and have them say it back. It is a habit, and habits are built by repetition, not by argument.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: Find the pair before reading, not during
teacherNotes.note: Left-to-right letter-by-letter reading breaks on these words, because the learner commits to the first letter's sound before they have seen the second. The move is to scan the word for the pair first. A finger under the pair is enough. It looks like a crutch and it is the skill.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.note: From here to the end of the level there are always more letters than sounds. A learner who counts letters will write a spare letter into every word. Have them say the word and count on their fingers before they write.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: ir, er and ur are one sound with three spellings
teacherNotes.note: Unit 18 adds ur, so a learner who meets ir and er here as arbitrary is ready for the third. Say plainly that the spelling cannot be heard and must be seen. Adults find this less upsetting than children do, but only if you say it outright rather than letting them discover it by getting it wrong.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: hear and hair need meaning, not phonics
teacherNotes.note: Both decode correctly and a learner can read both and still use the wrong one. Anchor them to the body: ears hear, heads have hair. The practice is a gap fill for that reason — it tests the meaning the decoding cannot reach.

teacherNotes.note: A learner who has reached here can read most one-syllable English. That is the hardest part of the whole level and it is behind them. Say so. Book B adds no new sounds at all, only new spellings for sounds they already have, and knowing that changes how the next six units feel.
